title: Describe the Painting
description: Brute force to optimized: touching every unit position along the range versus a difference map at segment boundaries, sorted and swept once.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: There is a 1D line painted with segments, each [start, end, color], where overlapping segments have their colors summed together. Split the entire painted range into the fewest maximal non-overlapping pieces such that within each piece, the combined color is constant, and return each piece as [start, end, mixedColor].

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Given overlapping colored segments (where overlap means the colors add together), determine the resulting combined color across the entire painted range, split into the fewest pieces of constant color.

blocks.title: Analogy: Mixing Overlapping Colored Light Beams on a Wall
blocks.text: Picture several colored light beams shone onto a wall along a single line, where their colors ADD together wherever they overlap (like mixing light, not paint). The wall's appearance only changes right where a beam begins or ends; describing the wall means listing each stretch of constant combined color.

blocks.caption: Mark +color at start, -color at end; the running sum between two points gives that stretch's combined color

blocks.text: The combined result is [[1,4,14],[4,7,16]]: from 1 to 4, colors 5 and 9 combine to 14; from 4 to 7, colors 7 and 9 combine to 16.
Before checking every unit-length position along the line, notice that the combined color only changes at a segment's start or end, exactly the difference-array/sweep-line technique.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A segment [start, end, color] contributes +color starting at "start" and -color starting at "end," exactly like the difference array technique used for range updates.

Observation 2: Recording these marks in a map keyed by position, then sorting the distinct positions, identifies every point where the combined color could possibly change.

Observation 3: Sweeping through these sorted positions while maintaining a running sum reconstructs the exact combined color across every stretch between two consecutive positions.

Observation 4: Any stretch with a running sum of 0 represents an unpainted gap and should be skipped in the output.
This leads to marking each segment's start and end as difference-map entries, sorting the distinct positions, and sweeping through to emit a piece for every nonzero stretch.
Conceptually, check every unit position along the entire range directly, summing the colors of every segment covering it.

items: Determine the overall range covered by all segments.
For every unit position in that range, sum the colors of every segment covering it directly.
Group consecutive positions with the same combined color into output pieces.

codes.python:
def split_painting(segments):
    min_x = min(s[0] for s in segments)
    max_x = max(s[1] for s in segments)
    colors = [0] * (max_x - min_x)
    for start, end, color in segments:
        for x in range(start, end):                 # touch every unit position directly
            colors[x - min_x] += color

    result = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(colors):
        if colors[i] == 0:
            i += 1
            continue
        j = i
        while j < len(colors) and colors[j] == colors[i]:
            j += 1
        result.append([min_x + i, min_x + j, colors[i]])
        i = j
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every unit position in the overall range is touched directly, summing every covering segment's color.
With coordinates potentially up to a billion, this is only feasible when the range itself is small.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(range times segments.length) in the worst case.
Space: O(range) for the per-position color array.

Limitation: the combined color only ever changes at a segment boundary, so touching every unit position, most of which see no change at all, is unnecessary and impractical for large coordinate ranges.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why touching every position is wasteful: the combined color is constant between any two consecutive segment boundaries; only those boundaries themselves need to be considered.

What replaces it: a difference map keyed by position, marking +color at every segment's start and -color at every end.

How to reconstruct the pieces: sort the distinct positions in the map, sweep through them maintaining a running sum, and emit a piece [current position, next position, running sum] whenever that sum is nonzero.

The core idea: mark segment boundaries in a difference map, sort just those positions, and sweep once to emit every constant-color piece.

For every segment [start, end, color], add color to a map entry at start, and subtract it from the entry at end. Sort the map's distinct positions. Sweep through them, maintaining a running sum; between each pair of consecutive positions, if the running sum is nonzero, emit [current position, next position, sum] as an output piece.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: difference map at boundaries, sort, sweep, emit nonzero pieces

blocks.text: Marking +color at a segment's start and -color at its end means a running sum swept across sorted positions correctly reflects the combined color at every point, since each segment's contribution is included exactly between its start and end. Since the combined color cannot change except at one of these marked boundaries, sweeping through only the distinct marked positions (not every unit position) correctly identifies every constant-color piece.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), sorting the O(n) distinct boundary positions.
Space: O(n) for the difference map.

blocks.text: Describe the Painting is a direct application of the sweep-line difference technique: mark only where color changes (segment boundaries), sort those marks, and sweep once to reconstruct every constant piece, entirely independent of how large the coordinate values themselves are.

items: Forgetting to skip stretches where the running sum is 0 (unpainted gaps), which should not appear in the output.
Using an array indexed by raw coordinate value instead of a sorted map of only the boundary positions, which fails for large coordinate ranges.

blocks.text: Recognizing this as a sweep-line/difference-array problem, "mark where color changes, not every position," is the key insight to state clearly before coding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "coordinates can be huge, how do you avoid an array over the whole range", think: a difference map keyed only by segment boundary positions, swept in sorted order.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(range times segments.length) time and O(range) space. The optimized difference-map sweep runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space, independent of the coordinate range.

items: Pattern: a sweep-line difference map, marking color changes only at segment boundaries.
Core Idea: mark +color at each segment's start and -color at its end; sort the distinct boundary positions and sweep once, emitting a piece for every nonzero stretch.
Time: O(range times segments.length) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(range) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the combined color only changes at segment boundaries, making a difference map over just those points sufficient, regardless of the coordinate range.
Interview Difficulty: a clean sweep-line application once the difference-array framing is recognized.
One line memory trick: difference map at boundaries, sort, sweep, emit nonzero stretches.
